outcome: Operating method 2. Unmeasured.

instruction: Time-box every step (the orchestrator charter says five minutes; the card and directive #48 tightened this to three). At the budget, write progress and return INCOMPLETE with the exact remainder; re-cut an over-budget step, never extend it.
outcome: The five-minute budget was superseded by three minutes (#48). The watchdog flags any agent over 3 minutes with no result.

instruction: For each stage, produce the step plan (id, kind, goal, inputs, outputs, check, job) from the card, the design, the task DAG and the context file. Sequence by dependency and lane, and keep every seat productive.
outcome: Duty 1 (manage tasks). Unmeasured.

instruction: Run a watchdog tick that flags steps over budget, orphaned waiters (kill them), dead machine jobs, load above 30 and more than two testers. Fix the mechanical yourself and prescribe the rest as exact commands.
outcome: Directive #43. The watchdog kills session shells polling for over 10 minutes and logs FIXED to the ledger.

instruction: Order mid-run edits to dispatched lane keys only. A file no lane owns goes to the lane whose diff broke it, with an explicit grant, never to 'orchestrator'. One writer per file per round.
outcome: D142: one design line was ordered to the orchestrator six times (D119 to D140) and never landed, because the orchestrator-fix step edits only lane-owned files.

instruction: When a REVISE needs an orchestrator act (a commit, a tick, a board edit) before the next judge can score, name no lane key in it. Fold lane edits into the orchestrator's list or a later round.
outcome: D92: a lane-keyed correction kept the accept loop running, so the PO re-accept (37 calls) and the next judge scored an uncommitted tree.

instruction: Before assigning row work or a REWORK's owed edit to a lane, ls each path and grep the design and tasks files for its owner. Name each owner; an unowned or other-lane file gets its ownership line in the same ruling.
outcome: D139/D161: D137 put three defects in a lane whose fixes landed in another lane's files.

instruction: Before relying on a scheduler property (FIFO order, slot, timeout), open the function that implements it and name the line. Size a battery against the verifier window (rows x per-row seconds from the last log).
outcome: D159: a ruling said 'never kill, a relaunch loses its FIFO place', but the lock claims by a bare mkdir race before consulting the waiter list, so another suite took the freed slot ahead of the head waiter.

instruction: Execute exactly one step and return its result in the shape the prompt asks for.
outcome: Lean step-worker charter. Unmeasured.

instruction: Pay ceremony once per file changed. Before opening a branch, find every open card that touches the same files and absorb them into ONE branch, keeping each id as an acceptance row (one fix doc, one coverage matrix, one battery, one gate).
outcome: 137 open cards (17 with branches, touching 36 lib/ files) collapsed by union-find into 7 provably disjoint components. Six cards in one auth service file became one change reviewed once.

instruction: When choosing a batch of disjoint branches, take the smallest footprint first. A wide invariant branch gets a round of its own.
outcome: A wide branch locks out everything it touches and starves the round.

instruction: Ration a shared resource by the resource actually contended: devices by device locks, not by test slots.
outcome: legs.sh rationed device legs by suite slots, so two-till legs were refused while both tills sat idle.

instruction: Release a directory lock by deleting its named stamp file first, then rmdir.
outcome: A lock leaked on every path because rmdir only removes empty directories.

instruction: If a lock path that should be a directory is a file, refuse loudly. Never work around it.
outcome: A train.lock left as a file reading 'STATE: RELEASED' made mkdir fail forever. A released lock blocked the merge door for 35 minutes, twice.

instruction: Judge liveness by last activity (mtime) or by the owning agent, never by a recorded pid. Every Bash call is a new shell.
outcome: A recorded pid dies within minutes and looks like an orphaned lock. Near-miss 2026-09-08: the next reader could break a LIVE train's lock and merge into main underneath it.

instruction: Run one requirement's whole delivery ladder (probes -> develop -> certifier in parallel with judge -> one rework -> re-certify -> small train) as ONE resumable workflow script. The PO acts only at rulings and the merge go.
outcome: Owner directive #40. Template control flow was dry-run verified 2026-09-05: the happy, one-rework and API-death paths all reach MERGED.
owner_words: deeper and smarter, not at cost of quality

instruction: Run mechanical preconditions before any launch: directive enforcement live, board state, machine load < 30, fewer than 2 live heavy test runs, card has its acceptance list, branch/worktree state known.
outcome: Takes two minutes, all scripted.

instruction: Paste a workflow template inline into the Workflow script input. Never Write it to a file first.
outcome: No measurement given.

instruction: Before launching a workflow, dry-run its control flow: wrap the body in an async IIFE with stubbed agent/parallel. A bare node --check rejects the top-level return the runtime allows.
outcome: Verified 2026-09-05: the happy, one-rework and API-death paths all reach MERGED.

instruction: Every agent's final answer is a structured result object, so the script, not a human, decides the next stage.
outcome: Removes the PO turn between stages (#40).

instruction: Do not dispatch one long-running agent per stage (40-100 minutes each). Break stages into short steps.
outcome: Template v1 retired. On 2026-09-08 four of six stages overran, and the two that did not ran no battery.

instruction: Cap every dispatched step at a fixed short budget (5 minutes here, later 3). Note the start time; at ~90% of the budget stop, write progress to disk and return INCOMPLETE with the exact remainder. Never overrun to 'just finish'.
outcome: A step lost to a kill costs only its budget. Budget later tightened to 3 minutes (CLAUDE.md #48).
enforcement: date +%s self-timing; watchdog.sh; tool_guard LENGTH (per CLAUDE.md)

instruction: Use three step kinds. llm: one narrow piece of thinking or editing. machine: launch a job in the background with nohup, a log and a pid, then return. wait: a cheap check of pid/log.
outcome: The haiku wait agent was later replaced by scripts/pipeline/jobs_wait.sh in a one-call step (CLAUDE.md: 'never an agent that re-checks').

instruction: Every step reads the requirement's context file FIRST and appends its own section of 10 lines or fewer ('## <step id> — <verdict>') LAST. The ledger is the outcome record; the context file is the memory.
outcome: From the skill: a step that skips either half 'has broken the contract'.
enforcement: RULES text in every prompt; stage verify step checks a section per step

instruction: Give every step a contract: inputs, outputs, ONE check command whose exit code proves the step, its kind, and one ledger JSON line {ts, req, step, verdict, minutes, outputs}.
outcome: Makes each step independently checkable.

instruction: Start every stage with a planning step. It turns the goal into ordered short steps with contracts, grouping ~8-10 task-DAG nodes or one AC/failure class/gate per step, reads only what it needs, writes the plan into the context file, and does no work.
outcome: The stage's plan becomes reviewable data before it runs.

instruction: Plan every suite, battery, build or install as a machine step followed by wait steps. Nothing is ever busy-waited by an agent.
outcome: No measurement given.

instruction: The planning step lists every ruling needed BEFORE the stage runs (an AC naming a mechanism or proof shape, a missing acceptance list, a dependency not on main, an impossible device leg), each with a recommended answer. An empty list means the stage may run.
outcome: Moves rulings ahead of execution.

instruction: An INCOMPLETE step's remainder becomes the next step, continuing from disk. BLOCKED ends the stage at a ruling point.
outcome: No measurement given.

instruction: Run the certifier and the judge in parallel on a MUST delivery.
outcome: Owner directive #33 (throughput).

instruction: Keep a small train to at most four branches.
outcome: No measurement given.

instruction: Count live heavy test runs with one script, never with a pattern pasted into prompts. Count runs, not worker processes or shells that quote the pattern.
outcome: Counting failed twice in opposite directions on 2026-09-08. pgrep counted 4 workers per compliant run, so agents slept for nothing; the driver-pattern match counted a train's own wait-loop shell.

instruction: Above load 30 or with two heavy runs live, back off with a plain sleep. Never a polling loop, tail -f, or waiting on a background job.
outcome: Later replaced by 'never wait in the foreground' (CLAUDE.md #48, tool_guard WAIT).

instruction: The step that launches a battery, gate or analyzer job returns INCOMPLETE immediately with the log path. It never sleeps on, tails or polls its own job; a separate later step cites the log.
outcome: 2026-09-08: an agent read 'collected later' as 'wait, then collect' and spent 43 minutes in a sleep loop on a 3-minute step. Four of six stages overran.

instruction: Never name a script unconditionally in a dispatch prompt if it may not exist on the agent's tree. Give a fallback chain and have the agent ls first.
outcome: On 2026-09-08 the REQ-136 train reported being told to run a wrapper that was not yet merged and did not exist on main.

instruction: Launch one workflow run per requirement, never one script holding many, so a kill or ruling on one never stalls the others.
outcome: No measurement given.

instruction: Keep one requirement in flight per track, with no stage skipped; the artifacts are the contract trail.
outcome: No measurement given.

instruction: The product owner's heartbeat picks the next item, never a prompt from the owner.
outcome: No measurement given.

instruction: Keep one shared, singular product owner across parallel teams, owning priority, the board and done-ness. Never duplicate it.
outcome: One head holding the whole board caught REQ-037/042 as one defect, and REQ-042's unmeetable AC before its branch was cut.

instruction: Assign work by lane (the source file a branch edits), not round-robin. Two requirements in one lane never run in parallel.
outcome: Breaking the lane rule produces two branches editing one file.

instruction: Give a free team the highest-priority READY item from a free lane. If every free lane is blocked, take a lane-free item (tooling, docs, gates) rather than idle.
outcome: No measurement given.

instruction: Allow at most one highest-risk (money-path) change in flight pipeline-wide, regardless of team count.
outcome: No measurement given.

instruction: Only the product owner writes shared files (requirements, order, lessons, domain, charters). Teams write only their own artifacts, code and activity-log entry.
outcome: CLAUDE.md method 6 adds: a file two agents write is a deadlock.

instruction: Maintain a dependency DAG of open requirements, every edge a real constraint (dependency, lane, tier, rig) with its reason. Publish a ready set at least N+1 deep.
outcome: A team finishing early takes its next item without waiting on a heartbeat.

instruction: A team blocked mid-item parks it back on the ready set and takes the next item. Blocked work is parked, not staffed.
outcome: No measurement given.

instruction: If the ready set cannot stay 3 deep, escalate with remedies (re-tier, split, promote a lane-free finding, reorder) rather than idle.
outcome: An over-serialised backlog is an escalation, not an excuse.

instruction: All delivery flows through a team. No ad-hoc side channel; the orchestrator never 'just quickly' does a stage itself. A stage that seems skippable is recorded on the item and stays owned.
outcome: A separate 'tooling slot' track was abolished.

instruction: On resume, before dispatching anything: read the state file, the lessons, domain and pipeline docs; reconcile against the repo (worktrees, branches, log, rig lock); trust the repo and correct the state file; dispatch every team before replying.
outcome: Subagent context dies with the session; the artifacts carry continuity.

instruction: No idle agent. Run each team as a pipeline (analyst on item n+2, architect n+1, developer n, tester n-1), never more than two stages ahead of the developer. A stage with no input takes the next item's earlier stage.
outcome: Analysis further ahead goes stale and can be invalidated by an upstream ruling.

instruction: Before ending any turn, confirm every team has live work and dispatch before replying. Recording an assignment is not dispatching it.
outcome: Mistaking a recorded assignment for a dispatch cost a pod one full cycle.

instruction: While any requirement sits at DESIGNED or ANALYSED, dispatch no new analysis or design. Drain the backlog to MERGED first.
outcome: Owner directive #27.
owner_words: dont put anything in analysis on design - po unless all designed and analysed are fixed and merged.

instruction: Merge in trains: compose with merge-tree first, run ONE full gate on the composed tree, merge in order, retire each branch.
outcome: Owner directive #30.

instruction: Staff each team with four developer seats, each holding a designed item (a rework counts), all loaded before ending a turn and recorded on the dashboard. Seats are long-lived agent runs, not one workflow.
outcome: Owner accepted the spend-limit exposure. CLAUDE.md #37 later reduced this to one active pod.
owner_words: looks like i have very less developers, each pod should have 4 developers each.

instruction: Dispatch preflight: before spawning a stage that books owner time, a device or the battery, paste the artifact checksum and the smoke checksum into the prompt. If they differ or the smoke is absent, dispatch the smoke instead. Log a DISPATCH line BEFORE the spawn.
outcome: An owner login round and a 6-leg battery were spent on a build that failed 5/5 on first launch.

instruction: Keep working scratch in a gitignored directory inside the repo, never in system tmp. Commit what a later agent must read; remove resources only when their own task succeeds; a killed task's files are its successor's starting point.
outcome: Owner directive #32: nothing is lost to an interruption.

instruction: Move tooling that mechanises recurring failure classes to the front of the queue.
outcome: REQ-136/137/138 jumped the queue.

instruction: Cap agents in flight at ten; queue the rest in the state file and dispatch as seats free.
outcome: Both the spend limit and the machine fail above ten, and a kill loses every agent at once.

instruction: Allow at most TWO heavy test runs machine-wide; the device runner has priority. Hold suite-running dispatches while load is above 30.
outcome: Load average hit 137 when four concurrent suites starved the emulators and adb.

instruction: A machine-wide lock uses a FIXED absolute slot directory (never TMPDIR-relative). An unusable directory is a loud refusal (rc 78), never a silent fallback.
outcome: A resumed session and an ssh login live in different bootstrap namespaces and would each hold their own pair of slots.

instruction: Never run the spec tool's bundled scripts that write a repo-global 'active feature' pointer. Set the feature directory (specs/<REQ>/) yourself.
outcome: With many agents running at once, a global mutable pointer silently clobbers between agents.

instruction: Size every task at AT MOST 30 seconds of work; split until it fits. The splitting is the analysis.
outcome: A node too big to state in 30 seconds hides dependencies inside it, which makes a 'dependency-ordered' list quietly wrong (constitution principle XIV).

instruction: Write each task as a checklist line '- [ ] T001 [P] [US1] Description with exact file path'. Use [P] only for truly parallel tasks and [USn] only in user-story phases.
outcome: Upstream Spec-Kit format.

instruction: End tasks.md with a fenced dag block, one line per task: 'id <secs>s <deps|-> <description naming the file>'. Every checkbox task appears exactly once; every edge is a REAL dependency (preference goes in [P], not edges); order is computed, not authored.
outcome: A dependency-ordered LIST is advisory; a DAG is executable.

instruction: Run the DAG validator and paste its output. It refuses cycles, edges to missing nodes, over-cap nodes, checkbox tasks with no node (unscheduled work) and nodes with no task (work nobody will do).
outcome: A tasks.md without a valid DAG cannot be committed.

instruction: Every agent returns a typed, structured result (a JSON schema) that the orchestration script reads. Free text is never parsed for control flow.
outcome: Lets rules (progress, stop, REVISE) be decided by code instead of another agent.
enforcement: workflow schemas (GAPS, DEV, VERDICT, S.*, STEP)

instruction: Treat a run with no task node as a refusal (rc 2) unless the caller explicitly declares that the outcome has no task DAG (noTasks:true).
outcome: Earned in REQ-406 O2 round 15 (judge findings F4/F9): runs without a node bypassed the evidence guard.

instruction: Feed rulings just recorded back into the next worker prompt as binding.
outcome: Without this, the next step re-asks or contradicts the ruling.

instruction: Carry a judge's REVISE from an earlier pass into the next pass as explicit input (one writer per file). Keep it out of the audit prompt so a resumed run can replay the audit from cache.
outcome: Resumed runs do not pay for the audit twice.

instruction: Allow up to 3 continuation steps for the proof, each told to finish exactly what the last one left.
outcome: The proof completes across fresh capped steps instead of one long one.

instruction: Take lanes from the task file's own lane tags in DAG order, supplied by the caller. Never default to a lane set, because a default belongs to some other requirement.
outcome: Earned by Bugbot on PR #37: with default lanes, another REQ would tick nothing and still spend a judge.

instruction: Agents never edit task checkboxes. They report task ids, and a script ticks the boxes under a lock. Never let two agents edit one file.
outcome: A file two agents write is a deadlock (earned method 6).

instruction: Run lanes with disjoint files in parallel (two at a time), wave by wave in DAG order.
outcome: Parallelism without file conflicts.

instruction: A dependency on an owner-only task or a device leg (never ticked by agents) does not block a coding task. Treat it as satisfied and go on; that leg is owed separately.
outcome: Earned by REQ-323's first run: lane C reported 59 of 60 tasks 'blocked' and lane W 76, many waiting only on owner-only or device tasks, so the build ended after one step per lane.

instruction: REVERTED rule: do not stop a lane when its open count is at most skipped plus blocked.
outcome: The old stop rule (laneOpen <= skipped + blocked) quit at once on REQ-323. It was replaced by: stop only when the lane did nothing and nothing it holds is doable, and repeat passes while any pass ticks something.

instruction: A task waiting on an unticked ordinary-code task of ANOTHER lane is not yours yet: list it as blocked and go on.
outcome: Lanes keep moving instead of waiting.

instruction: Lane stop rules. Finished when no lane tasks are open. Stop for now when the step did nothing and every remaining task is skipped or blocked. Stop after two consecutive steps that finished nothing.
outcome: Bounded lane loops without premature exits.

instruction: Repeat build passes over every unfinished lane while a pass still ticks something (at most 4 passes).
outcome: Cross-lane dependencies resolve over several passes.

instruction: For a launch step, progress means a NEW job (a new pid). Re-reporting already-queued jobs is the waiting loop again, so the scheduler's waiter takes over.
outcome: Earned in REQ-306 (model-s1 -> s2, 2026-10-07): a launch continuation only re-reported queued jobs.

instruction: Treat side tracks (already-specified work running alongside) like lanes: develop, verify, fix until no blocking findings, then judge at a gate.
outcome: No unjudged side work.

instruction: Resume a stopped run at a later stage from the recorded outputs of stages that already passed their judges. Never pay for them twice, and never regenerate an existing file: revise it in place. A build can also resume at a named wave.
outcome: REQ-323 stopped at tasks on 2026-10-06 after its spec, design and plan had passed.

instruction: Run the full swarm in fixed stage order: criteria, spec, design, plan, tasks, build (lanes in waves), accept, with a judge gate on every stage.
outcome: The owner protocol as code (#54-#62).

instruction: The architect writes a design of at most 500 lines: components, seams, data flow, file-level ownership and a test strategy (including goldens for every reference shot). Extend existing code only, and cite file:line.
outcome: A design grounded in the existing code.

instruction: The team lead reviews the design against the spec and the repo's hard rules and fixes defects in place with a dated note at the top. It then splits the work into lanes with DISJOINT file ownership, grouped into waves where a lane depends only on earlier waves: at most 6 lanes and 3 waves, typed by language.
outcome: Disjoint ownership enables parallel lanes without conflicts.

instruction: Generate the plan with the spec-kit plan skill from the spec and design, at most 300 lines. Do not change the design; record any defect under 'Plan findings'.
outcome: Keeps one source of design truth.

instruction: Generate tasks with the spec-kit tasks skill. Each task is at most 1 minute of work and at most 30 seconds by the validator: one file, one behaviour, the RED test before its code, tagged with exactly one lane key. Include the dag block, and re-run the DAG validator until it exits 0.
outcome: A machine-checked task DAG; the gate refuses an invalid one.

instruction: The tasks judge checks coverage of every spec AC and design component, sizing, RED-first order and lane tags, and re-runs the DAG validator.
outcome: Every AC has tasks.

instruction: After a judge-directed fix, drop the lane's earlier verify verdict as stale so no later agent re-opens findings from an old result.
outcome: Ruling D100(3).

instruction: Never pause the pipeline for the owner's hands-on review. The review is a parallel input that may reorder the queue, and any defect it finds enters at the head, but it never gates a dispatch.
outcome: 'An idle pipeline is duration burned for no quality.' One train in flight at a time, so a hands-on finding always has a clean head to enter at.

instruction: Freeze an artifact once it passes its stage (design, plan). A defect found later goes into the owning lane's fix doc, not into another plan round.
outcome: Ends repeated plan rounds. REQ-306's plan froze at plan-r1.

instruction: Tasks name exact repo paths. A node naming a path that does not exist (e.g. a short 'research/...') would create a second copy of an oracle file.
outcome: No repo-root research/ existed. The no-duplicate directive (#54) forbids a second copy.

instruction: RED-first binds task nodes that add behaviour. Nodes that add only type declarations, scaffolding config or comments need no RED ancestor, but gain one the moment they get a branch, a computed value or I/O.
outcome: Five scaffolding nodes were released from a RED-ancestor bar they could never meet.

instruction: Every spec/plan/tasks artifact carries a 'Lessons:' line (none, or the lesson ids applied). The commit hook refuses the artifact without it.
outcome: A tasks.md that passed every other check was REVISE only because the commit door would refuse it.

instruction: When a task adds a member to an interface or abstract type, add one task node per implementer file and make every analyze or test node depend on all of them. A hidden compile dependency is forbidden.
outcome: Seven implements sites were found and five files would have been uncompilable after one node. This is the 'one site fixed, siblings bypass it' failure class.

instruction: Every artifact or bookkeeping act a ruling orders must have a named executor inside the workflow. If the same order has been given repeatedly with no executor, the orchestrator does it itself from the rulings.
outcome: A residuals file ordered three times (D51, D56, D75) had no executor. Commit (5) did not land because the workflow had no orchestrator turn between stages.

instruction: A bookkeeping-only REVISE names no lane, so the accept loop ends. Never re-run the PO and the judge on an uncommitted tree. Do ticks and commits by script and path, then run one final round of at most 5 calls that verifies only the delta.
outcome: The workflow dispatched fixdoc, then PO, then judge with no orchestrator turn, so verdicts landed on an uncommitted tree (tasks.md: 0 of 107 ticked).

instruction: A new RED or guard row extends the test that already pins the value. Grep for the existing pinning test first, and create a new file only if the grep is empty. A second scanner is duplicate code.
outcome: A task changed a line pinned by an existing test with no node owning the break, which invited a weakened test.

instruction: Development and fix steps never launch or wait on a battery or full suite. A verifier launches jobs, and a waiter script (not an agent that re-checks) waits for them.
outcome: 24 PENDING collect agents read 24.6M tokens. 16 continuations waited on their own jobs queued behind suite-slot holders.

instruction: Each file has one writer (one lane) per round. Settle cross-lane stalls with explicit ownership calls. An edit refused for a stale read is re-read, never forced.
outcome: A fix lane was BLOCKED on four writes outside its lane, and a hub file had no wave-3 owner. A lane-local edit to a shared rig would be re-conflicted at every lane sync.
enforcement: D142 rule (cited throughout); lane tables in design.md

instruction: When a lane stalls, check whether the stall is in the dispatch. If the developer has no work left, stop continuing it and route the remaining verifier, test-agent and PO items to those roles.
outcome: Seven Developer continuations and five duplicate COLLECTs carried only other roles' items, which the step cap forbids a Developer to do.

instruction: A developer step's remaining-work list (nodesLeft) holds only nodes of its own lane. Another role's work goes in notRun with the role named.
outcome: Seven foreign items in nodesLeft caused a no-progress continuation (508 KB, 6 calls, no edit), because the stepper continues while the list is non-empty.

instruction: Make the shared test-slot lock FIFO: an arrival claims a free slot only when no live earlier waiter exists, and a waiter counts only if its pid is alive and not recycled. Write the RED test first. Never raise the slot cap.
outcome: A battery that had been first waiter since 05:47 still read '2 ahead', because a chained job re-took each freed slot. An earlier ruling rested on a FIFO the code did not implement.

instruction: Dispatch a COLLECT only once the job log's last line matches the completion pattern ('All tests passed|Some tests failed'). Let the waiter own the wait, and classify finished logs before re-listing collects.
outcome: A lane continuation re-listed three COLLECTs and a finished node and never read the two logs that had finished.

instruction: Code on a merge tree that has no task node is removed before the merge GO (every change traces to a node). Untraced files get a task node added first.
outcome: Six untraced cut files were given task nodes. Newer-wins code without a node was ordered removed.

instruction: While a merge waits on an owner-only leg, build the cheap host checks it will need. This costs nothing on the critical path.
outcome: C16 visual states and the host printing flow were built before the GO instead of being backlogged.

instruction: Run an evidence guard before every evidence or judge launch. A node marked CLOSED-BY a ruling is a skip, never a retry or a new question. Put the guard in the tracked dispatcher, with a control proving skip and allow.
outcome: O2 evidence was re-dispatched r13, r15 and r16 on an unchanged tree. A fifth identical dispatch is a process defect.

instruction: An empty finding list is never a dispatch. A fix round with zero findings routes to grading or commit, or stops BLOCKED naming the empty list. Fix the router RED first.
outcome: 15 wasted Developer dispatches were each BLOCKED with 'empty findings'.
enforcement: router fix REQ (RED test: a zero-finding round yields a grade/commit step)

instruction: Every ruling that orders a dispatch names the actor. A dispatch only a session's memory enforces gets forgotten, so move it into code: the runner pre-checks the condition and performs the step itself before refusing the dependent stage.
outcome: Five rulings ordered a manual dispatch with no named actor, and none happened. Sessions 133-138 each returned BLOCKED on the same missing commit.
enforcement: pre-check gate in the runner script (req406-execute.js)

instruction: Work no lane owns goes to one orchestrator-fix step (or a direct step), scoped to exact files. Never widen a lane to absorb it.
outcome: The lane-scoped orchfix refuses base files, so a direct step was named.

instruction: Exactly one runner per lane worktree, enforced by a launcher lease (run id, session, time). Liveness means a process with cwd in the worktree, or the lease/HEAD/ctx changed within 10 minutes. LANE-BUSY means stop: no edits, no jobs. Prove it with a RED control. A rule in a brief is not enough.
outcome: The brief-only rule failed three times in about ten minutes (sessions 161, 162b, 3), and one duplicate killed a coverage job. Local CI ended RED while extra runners shared the machine.
enforcement: lease claim step in the lane launcher (req406-lane.sh) + RED control test

instruction: Launch at most one swarm/outcome workflow per session at a time unless it runs on its own machine (logged override).
outcome: Three swarms on one 4-core machine queued every test run behind two suite slots for hours (2026-10-07).

instruction: Use exactly one sanctioned bounded wait (≤170 s, inside the 3-minute step) as a single call that reports ALIVE/ENDED per job; never spawn an agent just to check whether a job finished.
outcome: Journals of two REQs held 24 collect agents spawned only to answer PENDING, reading 24.6M tokens; every chain ended UNVERIFIED.
enforcement: scripts/pipeline/jobs_wait.sh run by judged-swarm.js waitJobs; tests test_jobs_wait.sh

instruction: Treat a pid as not an identity: a job is alive only while its pid runs AND that process (or a child) holds the job's log open or names it.
outcome: Pids recycle and restart from 1 after container restarts; a stranger inheriting the number was read as the live job.

instruction: Only batch branches into one gated tree when they touch disjoint source files; compute disjointness, never guess.
outcome: A dispatched round of four had three colliding pairs of six because one 12-file branch overlapped all siblings; the next round was disjoint by luck.
owner_words: he is making sure all devs stories dont impact each other and together they can be tested to save tokens

instruction: Before dispatching a round, pass four criteria as an exit code: prioritise cheapest-to-finish, keep every seat occupied with no duplicates, keep stories disjoint, and dispatch only stories with a heading and enumerated acceptance criteria.
outcome: Criteria were violated while believed; the first run of the checker found two cards under active dispatch with no board row at all.
owner_words: whether he is properly prioritising the tasks / he is making sure all devs are occupied / the stories are ready in form after passing through bsa and architect for dev to work upon

instruction: Do not dispatch work that cannot reach MERGED today (blocked on owner-only artifacts such as signing keys or credentials); check in milliseconds before spending an agent. Only merged is fixed.
outcome: A 12-agent workflow ran 68 min and 1.8M tokens on ten cards and merged zero: 23 of 103 owed legs were structurally impossible for any agent.

instruction: Never dispatch an absorbed card separately; one branch closes every card that is an instance of its invariant.
outcome: One defect was split across four cards and four ladders while ~830k tokens went to hand-driving the device rig, both already against policy.

instruction: Find branches whose tip is still their probe/RED-test commit and dispatch them first when finishing them would make current work cheaper.
outcome: That exact shape cost two hours on 2026-09-08: automation sat one Developer step from existing.

instruction: Treat other open cards naming the same source files as absorption candidates before dispatch.
outcome: Fragmentation of one seam across cards (directive #45).

instruction: Compute the review-ladder tier from the diff (money/sync/schema = full ladder; scripts/docs only = two agents), and name every existing branch for the item; never open a second branch for one card.
outcome: A card was dispatched as new work while a branch already edited the same file; the developer had to return BLOCKED to avoid two agents on one seam.

instruction: No two agents write the same file: each writes its own row file named for itself; the coordinator composes the shared dashboard.
outcome: Both merge trains of one day blocked at the merge door on a hot shared dashboard after gating cleanly: two complete gate runs spent on a file-locking problem.

instruction: Run a persistent watchdog that reports steps over 3 minutes, kills orphaned foreground pollers (>10 min) and stale test-slot holders, flags dead jobs, high load and more than two heavy runs; every event wakes the coordinator.
outcome: Every dispatch on one day carried a self-written 25- or 40-minute budget against real 7-51 min durations; a threshold nobody can meet is ignored, so this one fires.

instruction: Compose a one-screen health report from existing tools; report STALLED with evidence and the exact command, but never kill automatically.
outcome: Hand derivations cost ~1000 tokens each and were sometimes wrong (a stale lock read as a live train for four days; a grep -c guard that could never fire).

instruction: Judge agent liveness by the owning agent in the health watch, never by a pid recorded in a lock file.
outcome: Liveness by recorded pid was wrong within minutes (every hook invocation is a new shell).

instruction: Compute swarm compliance (judge gate passed before next stage, ctx read first, step length, no self-waiting) from workflow journals by script, and run a background stall-watch that wakes the session when a run is quiet for 20 minutes.
outcome: Compliance is facts, not opinion (directive #50); stuck runs had 48 agents, 18 idle, 0 judge calls.

instruction: Walk every branch to an end state: merged → retire; unmerged → catch up and check the door; merge-ready → train with full gate; blocked → one line naming the blocker. Never delete an unmerged branch and never merge on a red gate.
outcome: Thirteen open branches needed the same three mechanical steps; an agent is only for conflicts or missing coverage rows.

instruction: Ask the cheap authority (merge hook) N times first, then gate the tree that actually becomes main once; record main's sha before, revert the whole drain on red, and carry each card's door evidence in its --no-ff merge message.
outcome: The prior wave shape spent a ~12-minute gate on a composed tree the hook then refused, twice.

instruction: Gate N compatible changes once instead of once each, and verify main's final tree is byte-identical to the gated tree or revert (gate evidence applies only to the tree that became main).
outcome: Per-card trains re-ran the same ~3,400 tests eight times (1.6 h of repetition); the wave shape itself was later superseded by drain after its gates were spent on trees the hook refused.

instruction: Give each parallel lane its own derived verification tree (HEAD plus only that lane's files, its own scratch) so batteries run against its work only.
outcome: Three swarms sharing one tree: every battery of a relaunch ended rc 2 having run zero rows (other lanes' half-done code, edited targets, a shared scratch lock).

instruction: Validate the task DAG: one fenced dag block, every node at most 30 seconds of work naming its file, every edge a real dependency; implement in the printed order, resolving each dependency by implementing it.
outcome: A dependency-ordered list is advisory; a node that cannot be stated in 30 s hides dependencies that make an ordered list quietly wrong.

instruction: Classify open tasks by grep evidence (PRESENT/PARTIAL/ABSENT/NO-ANCHOR) and kind; evidence routes a task to verify-and-tick or build, never counts as proof; tick under a lock.
outcome: 255 of 340 boxes were open after an outcome run while earlier work sat done but unticked.
owner_words: complete all tasks in logical order

instruction: Keep the design role read-only: no worktree, branch, suite or gate run.
outcome: Architect BINDING; prevents contention for branches and slots.

instruction: Decompose every dispatch into PLAN / STEP / LAUNCH / COLLECT / COMMIT shapes of at most 3 minutes; a LAUNCH step never sees its own job's result.
outcome: PO BINDING; long budgets ran 7-51 min.

instruction: Compose large specs and task lists from fragments with a generator; edit fragments, never the generated file.
outcome: A 1,345-line spec and 3,837-line task list stay consistent; the composer asserts cross-outcome edges.

instruction: Put full runs (suite, battery, baseline, gates, capture) in separate LAUNCH and COLLECT DAG nodes; test runs inside a node are targeted file lists through the slot wrapper.
outcome: No task runs longer than 5 minutes (owner, REQ-406).
owner_words: no tasks with runtime more than 5 mins.

instruction: Plan headers state branch, tree read, diff baseline for every 'unchanged' check, 'planning only' (no code changed), revision notes and prejudge stamp; citations carry 'file:line, re-read <date>' and say whether the code graph was used.
outcome: Makes plan claims reproducible against a named tree.
